data.title: Gilead spends $1.28bn on PepStar’s potential Icotyde rival
data.description:
Gilead Sciences has inked a billion-dollar deal with Shanghai-based PepStar therapeutics to secure the global rights to an oral IL-23 receptor inhibitor, which the company hopes will rival Johnson & Johnson’s recently approved therapy Icotyde (icotrokinra). 

Through this deal, Gilead will hand over $1.275bn upfront to obtain the rights to PepStar’s macrocyclic peptide IL-23R inhibitor pill programme. This includes its lead asset, HCXT-2001, which is currently in Phase I trials. While the IL-23R inhibitor class has thus far made its commercial mark in plaque psoriasis, clinical success is now being seen in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Gilead is prioritising the latter with HCXT-2001, though the company is yet to specify which specific indications it will pursue. 

Unlike other options on the market, HCXT-2001 has an extended half-life, leading Gilead’s CMO, Dietmar Berger to claim that the drug could offer a “potentially differentiated approach” to the company’s burgeoning inflammation pipeline – which is primarily focused on IBD, type 2 inflammatory diseases, lupus and B cell-mediated autoimmune diseases. 

“We see potential for HCXT-2001 alone or in combination, including with emvistegrast, as a daily oral treatment for people living with IBD,” Berger added.  

Emvistegrast is Gilead’s in-house developed α4β7 integrin inhibitor, which is currently in mid-stage development for IBD. The drug has already demonstrated its potential, having recently met its primary endpoint in patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) during the Phase II SWIFT study (NCT06290934). 

According to Jefferies analysts, this deal is a good move from Gilead as it allows the company to pursue a promising combination. “Proof of concept data from ABBV-266 [a combination of risankizumab and trosunilimab] shows that a4b7 + IL-23 may offer the best clinical remission in patients with prior advanced treatment,” they commented. 

Meanwhile, they add that preclinical pharmacokinetic studies have pointed toward the early favourability of HCXT-2001 versus Icotyde – pointing to early signs of the drug’s differentiated potential. 

Gilead doubles down on dealmaking 

Gilead’s deal with PepStar is the latest in a string of deals inked by the California-based pharma, which is currently preparing itself for several key patent expiries across its virology portfolio. 

To bolster its pipeline and bring new promising assets in, Gilead has inked three acquisitions in 2026. This includes its $7.8bn buyout of CAR-T specialist, Arcellx, as well as its takeovers worth up to $5bn and $2.2bn of antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) developer Tubulis and autoimmune T-cell engager (TCE) therapy-focused biotech Ouro Medicines, respectively. 

In the same vein, Gilead also recently forged a $1.9bn licensing pact with Vir Biotechnologies centred around next-generation TCEs for solid tumours. 

According to a recent report by GlobalData, parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, more than half of the 157 surveyed pharmaceutical professionals feel optimistic or very optimistic about industry growth within the next 12 months.

data.title: Boehringer and Microsoft collaborate to explore AI in clinical research
data.description:
Boehringer Ingelheim and Microsoft have entered a strategic collaboration to examine the use of AI in clinical research, beginning with studies in lung health.

The partnership focuses on evaluating digital patient twins, which are computer-based models of individual patients constructed from clinical and related data.

The companies intend to examine whether these models can forecast disease progression and anticipate patient outcomes under varying circumstances.

Initial work will assess the technical and scientific feasibility of the concept across several therapeutic areas through prototyping, modelling, and generating evidence.

Researchers will study advanced trial simulation, disease-progression and predictive outcome modelling.

The work includes testing whether computational models can support synthetic or hybrid control arms as alternatives to standard clinical control groups.

Synthetic arms rely entirely on existing datasets, whereas hybrid arms combine historical data with conventional control subjects.

According to the companies, the approach could cut the volume of participants assigned to control cohorts, streamline trial design, and hasten evidence gathering.

If successful, the methods may enhance drug development efficiency and allow more trial subjects to receive experimental treatments.

Microsoft Germany and Austria corporate vice-president and CEO Agnes Heftberger said: “The collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim brings together pharmaceutical and scientific expertise with Microsoft’s capabilities in AI and engineering.

“Germany is home to world-class pharmaceutical research and development. Together, we want to explore how technology could open new opportunities for clinical research.”

Beyond clinical modelling, the alliance covers data centre modernisation and technical security. Both organisations are examining further joint development initiatives across animal health, commercial processes, and technology infrastructure.

The initiative links with Boehringer Ingelheim’s broader internal adoption of Microsoft Copilot, accompanied by workforce training, governance measures, and technical infrastructure updates across its human pharmaceutical and animal health operations.

Last month, Boehringer Ingelheim and Envisagenics entered a research collaboration and option agreement that aims to validate tumour-specific targets for the development of precision therapies in solid tumours.

data.title: Celltrion and Kaigene sign $580m licence deal for KG013
data.description:
South Korean biopharmaceutical company Celltrion has acquired exclusive global development and commercialisation rights to Kaigene’s investigational monoclonal antibody, KG013, in a deal worth up to Won769bn ($580m).

The financial package includes an upfront payment alongside milestone payments tied to specific development, regulatory, and commercial targets.

Royalties on net sales remain separate from the package. Kaigene also retains an option to co-market the candidate in South Korea under the contract.

KG013 is a fully human antibody designed with femtomolar binding affinity and an extended half-life for long-acting subcutaneous delivery.

It targets A Proliferation-Inducing Ligand (APRIL), a signalling protein that sustains plasma cell survival and immunoglobulin production, to suppress harmful IgA and IgM antibodies.

Researchers are formulating the candidate to provide durable target inhibition at lower doses and across extended intervals, aiming to reduce the administrative burden for patients facing prolonged treatment.

The primary target indication is immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN), a progressive renal disorder characterised by the accumulation of damaging IgA-containing immune complexes that provoke kidney inflammation and tissue damage.

Through KG013, Kaigene is broadening its pipeline into IgA- and IgM-mediated autoimmune conditions following its earlier efforts in IgG-mediated disorders.

Kaigene CEO Minjae Shin said: “Kaigene is building a comprehensive portfolio of therapies for pathogenic antibody-mediated diseases, and we believe KG013 has the potential to become a best-in-class treatment for IgA- and IgM-mediated diseases.

“IgAN, our first planned indication, affects approximately 160,000 diagnosed patients in the US alone and is particularly common in Asian populations. Patients, including approximately 30,000 in South Korea, need highly effective treatments with durable benefits.

“By working with Celltrion, a partner with comprehensive infrastructure for the global manufacturing, development and commercialisation of antibody therapeutics, we aim to bring KG013 to patients worldwide and make a meaningful contribution to care in South Korea.”

Kaigene is a US-based biotechnology company which develops autoimmune therapeutics using multiple technology platforms, including NanoBx (Nanobody-based Brain Shuttle), oral peptide therapeutics, multispecific monoclonal antibodies, and PDEGs [pathogenic antibody degraders].

Celltrion is expanding beyond its core biosimilar operations into new drug pipelines through in-house research and external licensing agreements.

data.title: Roche’s pharma sales grow 7% but pipeline trimmed down
data.description:
Roche posted a healthy 7% growth for its pharmaceutical division in the first nine months of 2026, though the drugmaker discontinued several clinical programmes amid asset prioritisation.

Sales for Roche’s medicines reached CHF 36.2bn ($44bn) for the period, denoting just under 80% of the company’s total sales. The Swiss franc’s appreciation against the US dollar impacted results this year, though the exchange-rate became more favourable in Q3.

Despite geopolitical headwinds, Roche’s business still performed strongly. Pharma sales were fuelled by allergy med Xolair (omalizumab), haemophilia drug Hemlibra (emicizumab), Ocrevus (ocrelizumab) for multiple sclerosis, breast cancer treatment Phesgo (pertuzumab and trastuzumab), and ophthalmological blockbuster Vabysmo (faricimab). Combined, the five drugs brought in nearly half of the division’s total sales, growing 12% across the nine months compared to the same period last year.

The results make welcome viewing for investors given Roche is experiencing significant headwinds from patent expiries. Roche is not resting on its laurels, however, revealing a sweeping prioritisation of its pipeline, in an earnings call.

As per its presentation, nine compounds were removed from clinical development, the majority from Phase I trials. The headline asset shelved was RG6540, an off-the-shelf CAR T therapy obtained via Roche’s $1.5bn acquisition of Poseida Therapeutics in January 2025. In the call, Roche CEO Thomas Schinecker confirmed that the company was not moving away from the modality, just stopping work on the molecule.

Other indications involved in the pipeline trim include Alzheimer’s disease, atopic dermatitis, and obesity, among others.

Earlier this week, Roche expanded an agreement with China-based Hansoh in a $15bn mega deal, with development spanning multiple antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) programmes. The Swiss company has made a string of acquisitions and license agreements already this year to bolster its pipeline.

In the call, Schinecker was confident in the strength of both Roche’s pipeline and commercial portfolio. “We had a strong performance yet again, and we made significant portfolio progress,” he said, adding that the company has a “good line of sight for growth to the end of the decade and beyond.”

data.title: Retatrutide peptide: A quality-control checklist for sourcing research-grade material
data.description:
Few research compounds have drawn as much procurement traffic in the past two years as retatrutide. It is a single 39-residue peptide engineered to act on three receptors at once (GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon), and that triple-agonist design has made it a common reference material in receptor pharmacology, signaling and assay-development work. Demand has pulled in a long tail of sellers, and what arrives in the vial varies widely.

For a lab, the real question is not where to find a retatrutide peptide. It is how to confirm that the powder in the vial is the molecule on the label, at the stated purity and mass, free of contaminants that will skew an assay. This checklist covers what a procurement or QC lead should ask for, how to read the documents that come back, and which signals should end the conversation.

What the molecule is, and why that makes QC harder

Retatrutide is an investigational compound developed by Eli Lilly under the code LY3437943. It has not been approved by the FDA, and late-stage clinical trials are still evaluating it in metabolic disease. Anything sold outside that program is research-use-only (RUO) material, intended for in vitro laboratory work.

Structurally, it is not a simple linear peptide. Several non-proteinogenic residues and a lipid side chain sit on the backbone, and each one is a place where synthesis can go wrong.

Each modification creates its own family of likely impurities. An incomplete coupling at an Aib position yields a deletion sequence that can elute close to the main peak. A failed or partial acylation at Lys17 leaves a des-lipidated species with very different chromatographic behavior. Racemization, oxidation and incomplete deprotection add more. A supplier who understands the molecule knows these failure modes; a reseller of unbranded bulk lots usually does not.

The documents to demand before any purchase order

A lot-specific certificate of analysis

The certificate of analysis (COA) is the central document, and the first test is whether it is truly lot-specific. The lot number on the COA should match the lot number printed on the vial label. The test date should fall after the synthesis date and reasonably close to the ship date. If a seller sends the same COA for every order, or a COA with no lot number at all, the document says nothing about the material you received.

Ask for past batches too. Certificates for previous lots give you a track record: purity trends, net-content consistency, and whether the testing lab stays the same.

Independent third-party testing

In-house testing is a starting point, not a verification. The COA should come from an independent analytical laboratory with no financial stake in the result, and the lab should be named on the document. A COA on the seller’s own letterhead, with no outside lab identified, is a claim rather than evidence.

Reading the analytical package

HPLC purity

Reversed-phase HPLC with UV detection (typically 214–220 nm for the peptide bond) is the standard purity measurement. The reported figure is the area percent of the main peak relative to total integrated area. For a lipidated peptide of this size, research-grade material should sit at or above 99%.

When reviewing the chromatogram itself, not just the number, look for:

  • The actual trace. A COA that reports “99.5%” with no chromatogram attached cannot be checked.
  • Integration settings. Unusually high peak-width or threshold settings can hide small impurities near the main peak.
  • Peak shape. Heavy tailing or a shoulder on the main peak often signals a co-eluting deletion or diastereomer.
  • Run length. A gradient that ends shortly after the main peak elutes may miss late-eluting hydrophobic species, which matters for a fatty-acid-modified peptide.

Identity: why HPLC alone is not enough

A single sharp peak proves the sample is mostly one compound. It does not prove which compound. Identity confirmation by mass spectrometry, usually ESI-MS or MALDI-TOF, should show an observed mass consistent with the theoretical ~4731 Da, with the expected charge-state envelope for ESI. A mass shift of about 16 Da suggests oxidation. A loss matching the C20 diacid and linker points to failed lipidation. Ask whether identity was confirmed by MS or inferred from retention time against a reference standard, and weigh the answer accordingly.

Net peptide content

Purity and quantity are different measurements. A vial labeled 10 mg can contain material that is 99% pure by HPLC and still hold noticeably less than 10 mg of actual peptide, because lyophilized powder also contains counter-ions (commonly acetate or TFA) and residual water. Net-content testing, by amino acid analysis, quantitative HPLC against a standard, or nitrogen determination, tells you how much peptide is really there. For any quantitative work, such as dose-response curves or binding constants, this number matters as much as purity.

Endotoxin and sterility

For cell-based assays, bacterial endotoxin is a quiet source of bad data. Lipopolysaccharide contamination can activate innate immune signaling in many cell lines and produce responses that look like compound activity. A limulus amebocyte lysate (LAL) result, reported in EU per mg, should be on the COA. Sterility testing adds another layer of assurance for any material that will go into culture.

Heavy metals

Metal contamination from reagents or equipment can interfere with enzymatic and fluorescence assays. A heavy-metals panel rules it out.

Commercial signals worth checking

How a vendor sells also tells you a lot. When a lab is ready to buy retatrutide peptide, these are the commercial checks that separate a research supplier from a marketplace reseller:

  • Transparent per-vial pricing. Pricing should be stated per vial and per size, not hidden behind “contact for quote” for standard quantities.
  • RUO framing that is consistent. The listing, the label and the checkout should all say research use only. A seller using “pharmacy-grade” language or human-use marketing for an unapproved compound is signaling that it is not operating as a research supplier.
  • Buyer verification. Age gating and institutional details at checkout show a vendor that knows who its customers should be.
  • Normal payment channels. Payment only through odd or untraceable channels is a reason to walk away.

Red flags that should stop a purchase

  • No COA, or a COA available only “on request” after payment
  • One COA reused across every lot and every size
  • Prices far below the rest of the market for the same mass
  • No lot number on the vial
  • Pre-mixed liquid offered in place of lyophilized powder
  • Testing attributed to an unnamed lab

Format, storage and cold chain

Lyophilized versus pre-mixed

A peptide is most stable as a dry solid. Freeze-drying removes water under vacuum and leaves a low-moisture cake that resists hydrolysis, deamidation and microbial growth far better than any solution. Choosing to buy retatrutide as a lyophilized solid in a sealed glass vial gives the lab control over the solvent, concentration and timing of preparation. A pre-mixed solution from a seller adds unknowns: what diluent was used, how long it sat, and at what temperature.

Good material appears as a uniform white cake or powder. Collapse, visible moisture or discoloration point to a poor freeze-drying cycle or a compromised seal.

Storage on arrival

For longer-term storage, the standard guidance is a sealed vial kept at −20 °C, desiccated and protected from light. Lab practice should log receipt date, lot number and storage location so that every result traces back to a specific vial.

Shipping and the cold chain

Lyophilized peptides tolerate short ambient transit far better than solutions, but time in a truck is still time at uncontrolled temperature. Ask where the material ships from, which carrier service is used, and the cutoff for same-day dispatch. Multi-week international transit with customs holds is a real stability risk, especially in summer.

How one supplier lines up against the checklist

HEEZ Research is one example of a US-based supplier that publishes the kind of documentation described above. Its retatrutide (Reta) is sold as lyophilized white powder in sealed glass vials, in 10 mg and 20 mg sizes, priced from $100 for a single 10 mg vial.

On the analytical side, every lot is sent to an independent third-party laboratory, and lot-specific COAs are published, including those for past batches. The listed tests cover HPLC purity and identity, net content, heavy metals, sterility and endotoxin. The stated purity specification is ≥99% by HPLC, and recent published lot results came in at 99.77% for the 10 mg vial and 99.60% for the 20 mg vial.

On the commercial side, orders placed before 2 PM ET Monday through Friday (1 PM ET Saturday) ship the same day from the USA by UPS 2nd Day Air or UPS Overnight, and nothing ships on Sundays. Buyers must be 21 or older, and checkout asks for an institution name and a matching institutional email. All sales are final, and the material is sold for in vitro research use only, not for human or veterinary use.

For labs running related receptor work, the same documentation standard applies across the vendor’s wider catalog of research-grade peptides, so one QC review process can cover several compounds.

A short procurement checklist

Before approving an order, the reviewer should answer yes to each:

  1. The COA lot number matches the vial label.
  2. A named, independent lab did the testing.
  3. HPLC purity is ≥99%, chromatogram attached.
  4. Identity was confirmed, ideally by MS, against ~4731 Da.
  5. Net content was measured, not assumed.
  6. Endotoxin, sterility and heavy metals are reported.
  7. The product is lyophilized in a sealed vial.
  8. Shipping is domestic and fast.
  9. Labeling is consistently research use only.

FAQ

What purity should a research-grade retatrutide peptide have?

At least 99% by reversed-phase HPLC, backed by a chromatogram and a lot-specific COA, with identity and net content also reported.

Is an HPLC result enough to confirm identity?

No. HPLC shows how much of the sample is a single component, not which component it is. Mass spectrometry confirms that the observed mass matches the theoretical ~4731 Da molecule.

Why does net peptide content differ from the vial’s labeled mass?

The powder also contains counter-ions and residual moisture. Net-content testing measures the actual peptide, which quantitative work depends on.

Why does endotoxin matter for an in vitro study?

Endotoxin can trigger signaling responses in many cell lines, producing effects that can be mistaken for compound activity. A low LAL result protects cell-based data from that artifact.

Should a lab accept pre-mixed retatrutide?

Better not. Lyophilized powder is more stable, while a pre-mixed solution carries unknown history.

How should lyophilized retatrutide be stored?

In its sealed vial, protected from light, at −20 °C with desiccation for longer-term storage. Log the lot number and receipt date for traceability.

What is the biggest red flag when sourcing retatrutide?

A COA with no lot number, or the same COA reused for every batch. Without lot-level documentation, there is no way to know what the vial actually contains.

data.title: AstraZeneca bags another US indication for Ultomiris with IgAN approval
data.description:
AstraZeneca has notched another indication to the belt of its rare disease therapy Ultomiris (ravulizumab) through an accelerated US approval in primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN), a type of chronic kidney disease. 

Following the US Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) call to initially greenlight Ultomiris in IgAN, the drug will provisionally be available to patients at risk of disease progression – specifically to reduce the presence of protein in the urine.  

Ultomiris’ accelerated approval stems from the Phase III I CAN trial (NCT06291376) in which the intravenously delivered C5 complement inhibitor prompted a placebo-adjusted 43.4% drop in the presence of excess urine proteins in IgAN patients at the 34-week mark.  

While the drug has already shown promise in reducing proteinuria, AstraZeneca is yet to establish whether Ultomiris can slow the functional decline of kidneys in IgAN patients. This means that Ultomiris’ full US approval in IgAN will hinge on whether the drug can demonstrate clinical benefit in the ongoing Phase III I CAN trial, in which researchers are evaluating the drug’s impact on the rate at which the kidneys filter blood. 

IgAN is a rare, progressive kidney disease that leads to the damage and destruction of cells in the glomeruli, which play an essential role in the kidney’s ability to filter blood. Currently, scientists estimate that around 2.5 in every 100,000 people worldwide are living with IgAN – of which approximately half have elevated levels of protein in their urine. 

With an accelerated approval secured, Ultomiris will join a competitive IgAN market, which is currently dominated by Asahi Kasei-owned Calliditas Therapeutics’ first-to-market therapy Tarpeyo (budesonide). However, Novartis’ therapy Fabhalta (iptacopan) which became the first approved complement inhibitor for this indication, is rapidly closing the gap, with the drug generating $505m in 2025 compared with Tarpeyo’s $517m in the same year.  

The competition is set to heat up further, however, as there are 22 ongoing Phase III studies in IgAN, according to GlobalData’s Pharmaceutical Intelligence Center. 

Recently, Roche’s potential Fabhalta rival sefaxersen met its endpoints in the Phase III IMAgINATION study (NCT05797610), while Vertex Pharmaceuticals is also seeking approval for povetacicept after the drug was successful in the late-stage RAINIER trial (NCT06564142). 

As per a recent report by GlobalData, parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, there are currently 112 molecules in the IgAN pipeline, with three in the pre-registrational phase and 40 in mid-to-late-stage development.

data.title: Podcast: The impact of prediction markets on the clinical sector
data.description:
Publicly traded drug developers have been exposed to insider trading on their stocks for decades, but with the introduction of prediction markets in the clinical sector private companies are now also at risk.

July 2026 saw the prediction market platform Kalshi offer something new: odds on the outcomes of clinical trials and drug approval bids. With drug development now opened to betting from the public, many have raised concerns over the ethical questions that follow. In this latest episode, Pharmaceutical Technology reporter Frankie Fattorini speaks with Chelsea Andeson and Noah Solowiejczyk—partners at the US law firm Fenwick—to discuss how these prediction markets also pave the way for new challenges in insider trading and how biotechs will have to adapt.

data.title: Astellas and AI Proteins sign miniprotein therapeutics deal
data.description:
AI Proteins has signed a research collaboration and licence agreement with Astellas Pharma’s affiliate Astellas Innovation Management for discovering and developing miniprotein therapeutics.

Under the deal, AI Proteins is set to receive an upfront cash sum of more than $400m to design and optimise de novo miniproteins directed at targets selected by Astellas.

AI Proteins also qualifies for milestone payments and royalties on net sales generated by resulting therapies.

AI Proteins president, CEO and founder Chris Bahl said: “Every biologic medicine on the market today is based on a molecule borrowed from nature that evolved to do something else.

“Designing miniproteins de novo lets us work from the other direction, meaning we specify what a medicine needs to do, then build a molecule from scratch to do precisely that.

“It’s a shift from repurposing to design, and it puts problems within reach that traditional biologics can’t solve. Astellas has deep expertise in translating innovative science into medicines, and they’re the right partner to carry this forward to patients.”

Astellas holds an exclusive global licence to therapeutic candidates produced through the partnership. The company will oversee all subsequent development, regulatory processes, and commercialisation.

AI Proteins will deploy its computational discovery platform to design proteins targeting multiple pathways to generate the candidates.

Astellas Innovation Lab senior vice-president Morten Sogaard said: “Our collaboration with AI Proteins reflects our strategic focus on strengthening our early-stage research pipeline through partnerships that provide access to novel biology, differentiated technologies and new therapeutic possibilities.

“By combining AI Proteins’ advanced de novo protein design capabilities with Astellas’ expertise in translating scientific breakthroughs into innovative medicines, we aim to accelerate the discovery of high-quality therapeutic candidates that can help fuel long-term innovation and support our pipeline-led growth strategy.”

data.title: MSD’s Keytruda and Padcev combination receives EC approval
data.description:
The European Commission (EC) has approved Merck & Co’s (MSD) Keytruda (pembrolizumab) plus Padcev (enfortumab vedotin-ejfv) as perioperative treatment for resectable muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) in adults.

The clearance permits the therapies to be administered before radical cystectomy as neoadjuvant therapy and continued following surgery as adjuvant treatment.

Applicable to patients irrespective of cisplatin eligibility, the authorisation covers Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and all 27 EU member states.

The regulatory decision also encompasses Keytruda SC, marketed in the US as Keytruda Qlex (pembrolizumab and berahyaluronidase alfa-pmph).

MSD research laboratories senior vice-president and oncology, global clinical development head Dr Marjorie Green said: “Building on the previous approval of Keytruda plus Padcev in the European Union less than six months ago, we’re pleased to bring this important treatment option to a broader patient population as the first PD-1 inhibitor plus antibody-drug conjugate regimen approved for people with muscle-invasive bladder cancer regardless of cisplatin eligibility.

“This approval represents encouraging progress in bladder cancer care and underscores our commitment to addressing the needs of people who are living with this disease.”

The decision follows a positive opinion granted last month by the European Medicines Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use.

The assessment was based on the open-label, randomised Phase III KEYNOTE-B15 study, also designated EV-304, conducted alongside Astellas and Pfizer.

In 808 patients, perioperative treatment lowered the risk of disease recurrence, progression, or death by 47% compared to neoadjuvant cisplatin and gemcitabine chemotherapy alongside surgical resection.

MSD stated that local availability across Europe will depend on country-level reimbursement processes.

The decision follows regulatory clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration in July 2026.

data.title: FDA approves GSK’s Hibsago as first functional cure for hepatitis B
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved GSK’s Hibsago (bepirovirsen), marking the first functional cure available to hepatitis B patients in the US.

The drug will be available for patients without cirrhosis, already receiving nucleos(t)ide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) therapy for at least six months who have suppressed HBV deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), and hepatitis B virus (HBV) surface antigen (HBsAg) levels below a certain amount. If patients meet these requirements, Hibsago is given alongside the NRTI therapy.

The approval marks a significant moment for US patients with the chronic form of the liver disease, who need to take daily antiviral pills or immune-modulating injections. Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by HBV. Over time, the infection can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and increase the risk of liver cancer.

Hibsago is the first FDA-approved antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to treat chronic hepatitis B, according to the agency. The drug netted its first regulatory approval in Japan in August 2026.

Hibsago works by targeting the genetic material of HBV in liver cells so it can be used by the virus to make viral proteins and support viral replication. This lowers the amount of virus and hepatitis B surface antigen in the body. Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks.

Results from GSK’s Phase III trials (NCT05630807; NCT05630820) demonstrated that 19% of patients had undetectable levels of hepatitis B virus after receiving the drug for half a year, indicating the disease is controlled by the immune system without medication. This is known as a functional cure, which is only achieved in around 1% of cases treated with standard of care (SoC).

GSK’s chief scientific officer, Tony Wood, said: “Despite current therapies, many people living with chronic hepatitis B remain on treatment indefinitely and continue to face the risk of serious liver complications. For the first time, with Hibsago, US patients have the potential to achieve functional cure after a six-month treatment course, with the added convenience of the option of self-administration after the first dose.”

While Hibsago showed acceptable safety and tolerability, the drug does come with two boxed warnings. One is the potential to cause serious liver reactions, and the other is its ability to cause low blood platelet numbers. In some cases, the latter – known as thrombocytopenia – can be life-threatening.

Citi analysts said the thrombocytopenia boxed warning was “less expected”, though they maintained a blockbuster sales prediction for the treatment, calling both warnings “manageable”.

GSK expects peak annual sales of more than £2bn ($2.68bn) for Hibsago, with the product a key driver to the drugmaker’s wider aims of reaching more than £40bn in annual revenue by 2031.

Analysis by GlobalData’s Pharma Intelligence Centre predicts Hibsago will become a blockbuster drug in 2032.

GlobalData is the parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology.
